samples.text:
Nowadays, many skilled workers like doctors and engineers leave developing countries to work in rich countries, because they can earn more money and have better conditions. This is often called brain drain. In this essay I will discuss the problems this cause for developing countries and suggest some solutions.

The biggest problem is that there are not enough professionals in the home country. For example, if many doctors move abroad, the hospitals in poor countries do not have enough staff, and patients must wait a long time or cannot get treatment at all. This is very serious in the countryside. Another problem is that the government lose the money which it spent on education. In many developing countries, university is free or cheap, so the country pay for training these doctors and engineers, but another country get the benefit. Also, without engineers and scientists, it is difficult for the country to develop new industries and improve the economy.

There are some ways to solve this problem. First, the government should increase the salaries and improve working conditions for professionals, so they will want to stay. For instance, hospitals need modern equipment and doctors should not work too many hours. Second, students who receive free education could be asked to work in their own country for some years after they graduate. Third, the government can encourage people who went abroad to come back, by giving them good jobs or other benefits. Finally, wealthy countries also have responsibility, and they should not take too many workers from poor countries.

In conclusion, brain drain causes a shortage of skilled workers, a waste of money and slower development. I think that developing countries should give professionals better conditions and reasons to stay in their homeland.
samples.why: Addresses problems and solutions with relevant ideas · limited development and some repetition · list-like linking (First, Second, Third) · adequate vocabulary · repeated subject-verb agreement errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
In recent decades, large numbers of highly trained professionals, including doctors, nurses and engineers, have left developing countries to work in wealthier nations, attracted by higher salaries and better working conditions. This so-called brain drain has serious consequences for the countries they leave behind, but there are measures that could reduce its impact.

The most obvious problem is a shortage of skilled staff in essential sectors. When doctors and nurses emigrate, hospitals and clinics in their home countries struggle to provide adequate care, and rural areas, which are already underserved, are usually the worst affected. The departure of engineers and scientists similarly slows the development of infrastructure and new industries. In addition, brain drain represents a significant financial loss. Governments often invest heavily in educating these professionals, only to see richer countries benefit from their skills without having paid for their training. Over time, this can widen the gap between rich and poor nations.

Addressing this problem requires both national and international action. Developing countries could make it more attractive for professionals to stay by improving pay, investing in modern equipment and offering clear career progression, since many people leave not only for money but because of poor facilities and limited opportunities. Some governments has also introduced schemes that require graduates of publicly funded courses to work in the country for a fixed period. Another approach is to encourage emigrants to return, or to share their expertise through teaching visits and online collaboration. At the same time, wealthy countries should recruit ethically, for example by avoiding active recruitment of health workers from countries facing severe shortages, and could contribute to training programmes in those countries.

In conclusion, the emigration of skilled professionals deprives developing countries of vital services and wastes public investment. Better conditions at home, return incentives and responsible recruitment by richer nations could together reduce the damage.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · problems in health, development and finance extended · solutions at national and international level · good vocabulary (underserved, recruit ethically) · mostly accurate with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The migration of skilled professionals from developing to wealthier countries is driven by understandable personal ambitions: higher salaries, better equipment and clearer career paths. Yet the cumulative effect of these individual decisions can be severe for the countries they leave, and mitigating it requires action from both sending and receiving nations.

The most acute consequence is a shortage of expertise precisely where it is most needed. Health systems in lower-income countries, already under strain, lose doctors and nurses they can ill afford to lose, with rural populations typically suffering most as the remaining staff concentrate in cities. The departure of engineers, scientists and academics likewise weakens a country's capacity to build infrastructure, innovate and train the next generation. There is also a significant fiscal dimension. Developing countries often subsidise higher education heavily, so each departing graduate represents a public investment whose returns are enjoyed elsewhere; in effect, poorer nations end up subsidising the workforce of richer ones. Over time, this can entrench global inequality.

Since the causes are largely economic and professional, the most effective responses address working conditions rather than simply restricting movement. Improving salaries, investing in facilities and creating transparent paths to promotion can persuade many professionals that a rewarding career is possible at home. Bonding schemes, under which graduates of state-funded programmes serve domestically for a set period, can secure a return on public investment, provided they are fair rather than punitive. Governments can also cultivate their diaspora, offering incentives for return and channels through which emigrants contribute knowledge remotely. Receiving countries bear responsibility too: adhering to ethical recruitment codes and co-funding training in source countries would help ensure that migration benefits both sides.

In conclusion, the loss of skilled professionals weakens essential services, wastes public investment and deepens global inequality. A combination of better domestic conditions, well-designed retention schemes and responsible recruitment abroad offers the most balanced solution.
samples.why: Fully addresses both parts with extended, nuanced ideas · responses targeted at the root causes and qualified · skilful cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (fiscal dimension, entrench, diaspora) · virtually error-free complex structures.
